week_headline: The gut-hormone connection is having a moment — estrobolome research is making menopause science far more interesting than anyone expected

top10.claim: Estrobolome explained : How your gut microbiome impacts menopause symptoms and why fibre matters
top10.verdict: The estrobolome — the collection of gut bacteria that help metabolise oestrogen — is a genuinely real and researched concept, and there is solid emerging evidence that gut microbiome composition influences circulating oestrogen levels, which could affect menopause symptoms. Fibre genuinely feeds the beneficial bacteria involved in this process, so the fibre angle is well-grounded. That said, most studies are still observational or in early stages, so while the direction of evidence is promising, we are not yet at 'eat more fibre and fix your menopause' territory — the clinical picture is more complex than headlines suggest.
top10.verdict_highlight: Real science, but still early-stage evidence
sources: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism — Baker et al. on estrobolome and oestrogen metabolism
Maturitas Journal — gut microbiome and menopause symptom research
NIH National Institute on Aging — microbiome and hormonal ageing studies
Nutrients Journal — dietary fibre and gut microbiota composition
EFSA — dietary fibre intake recommendations and gut health evidence
top10.global_opinion: In the US, functional medicine practitioners have enthusiastically embraced estrobolome messaging, sometimes ahead of the clinical evidence, leading to a boom in gut-hormone supplement marketing. In the UK, the NHS and NICE remain cautious, emphasising that menopause management should centre on evidence-based HRT and lifestyle rather than microbiome supplements until stronger trials exist. Japanese researchers have shown particular interest given Japan's traditionally high-fibre diet and historically lower rates of reported menopause symptoms, though separating diet from cultural reporting differences is methodologically tricky.
top10.brit_take: Lovely that your gut bacteria are finally getting credit for something other than causing embarrassment on the Tube. Just maybe hold off on the £60 probiotic subscription until the randomised trials catch up.
